title: Addressing Instrument–Outcome Confounding in Mendelian Randomization through Representation Learning
text: ICML 2026

title: Addressing Instrument–Outcome Confounding in Mendelian Randomization through Representation Learning
text:
The problem with genetic instruments
When randomized trials are infeasible or unethical, epidemiologists turn to Mendelian Randomization (MR): an instrumental-variable (IV) method (Angrist et al. 1996) that uses genetic variants as instruments for a risk factor, exploiting the fact that alleles are (in principle) assigned at conception independently of later-life confounders (Sanderson et al. 2022). A variable Z is a valid instrument for an exposure D with respect to an outcome Y, in the presence of an unobserved confounder H, when it satisfies three conditions:

Angrist, Joshua D., Guido W. Imbens, and Donald B. Rubin. 1996. “Identification of Causal Effects Using Instrumental Variables.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 91 (434): 444–55.

Sanderson, Eleanor, M. Maria Glymour, Michael V. Holmes, et al. 2022. “Mendelian Randomization.” Nature Reviews Methods Primers 2 (1): 6.

Relevance — Z is associated with D;
Exchangeability — Z \perp H;
Exclusion restriction — Z \perp Y \mid H, D.

Relevance is empirically checkable; exchangeability and the exclusion restriction are not, and are the ones that break in practice (Swerdlow et al. 2016).
Swerdlow, Daniel I., Karoline B. Kuchenbaecker, Sonia Shah, et al. 2016. “Selecting Instruments for Mendelian Randomization in the Wake of Genome-Wide Association Studies.” International Journal of Epidemiology 45 (5): 1600–1616.

The trouble is that in real genetic data the exchangeability condition is often violated. Population stratification and assortative mating make genetic variants and phenotypes share ancestry- and environment-driven influences, so the variant is no longer independent of the confounder, and the MR estimate is biased.
A worked example makes the failure concrete. Suppose we want the average causal effect (ACE) of type II diabetes (D) on coronary artery disease (Y), both confounded by unobserved population-level factors H. The candidate instruments Z = (Z_1, Z_2, Z_3) are each a mixture of latent sources U = (U_1, U_2,
U_3): U_2 and U_3 are stochastic recombination governed by Mendel’s law (valid), while U_1 is driven by population factors H (invalid). Because every observed variant mixes in a little of the invalid U_1, all of Z_1,
Z_2, Z_3 become invalid instruments, although two valid instruments are hiding inside.

Figure 1: A schematic of the entanglement problem. Latent sources (centre) generate the observed variants on the left; an invalid source (red, U_1) is influenced by the unobserved confounder H, so its leakage into every observed variant Z_1, Z_2, Z_3 renders all of them invalid. The green sources (U_2, U_3) would be valid if they could be isolated.



If we could recover the latent variables U from the observed Z, we would get back two valid instruments. That recovery problem is exactly an identification problem in representation learning.

title: Addressing Instrument–Outcome Confounding in Mendelian Randomization through Representation Learning
text:
A multi-environment setup
The key resource is that the same traits can now be studied across many populations: large biobanks such as All of Us (The All of Us Research Program Investigators 2019) make multi-environment data available. The underlying causal biology is shared across populations, but allele frequencies and linkage-disequilibrium structure differ by demographic history (Wang et al. 2020; Wang et al. 2023). So an observed variant can be read as a mixture of an invariant biological signal and an environment-specific confounding component.

The All of Us Research Program Investigators. 2019. “The ‘All of Us’ Research Program.” New England Journal of Medicine 381 (7): 668–76.

Wang, Y, J Guo, G Ni, J Yang, PM Visscher, and L Yengo. 2020. “Theoretical and Empirical Quantification of the Accuracy of Polygenic Scores in Ancestry Divergent Populations.” Nature Communications 11 (1): 3865.

Wang, Ying, Kristy Tsuo, Masahiro Kanai, and Alicia R Martin. 2023. “Polygenic Prediction Across Populations Is Influenced by Ancestry, Genetic Architecture, and Methodology.” Cell Genomics 3 (10): 100408.
This paper formalizes this. Across K environments one observes i.i.d. data \mathcal{D}_k = \{(Z_i^{(k)}, D_i^{(k)}, Y_i^{(k)})\}, where the candidate instrument is generated through an invertible mixing function Z^{(k)} =
f(W^{(k)}, V^{(k)}) from two independent latent blocks:

W^{(k)} — the valid part: W^{(k)} \perp H^{(k)}, and its distribution is invariant across environments;
V^{(k)} — the invalid part: V^{(k)} depends on H^{(k)}, and its distribution shifts across environments.

W and V need not be subvectors of Z — they are entangled through f and must be disentangled, not simply selected.
So while Z^{(k)} is invalid (because of V), there exists a map \varphi:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^p — the inverse of f onto the W coordinates — such that \varphi(Z^{(k)}) is a valid instrument.

Figure 2: The general setup. The observed instrument Z is an entangled mixture of a valid, environment-invariant component W (green) and an invalid component V (red) that shifts with the environment and is tied to the unobserved confounder H. Solid arrows are the data-generating mechanism; dashed red arrows are the confounding paths through V and H. Recovering W from Z restores a valid instrument for D \to Y.





Why recovering W up to a transformation is enough. Disentanglement does not remove the confounding between D and Y — that is what the instrument is for. It only recovers a clean instrument W so that IV machinery can be applied correctly.
The central object is the IV moment restriction: with the true causal parameter \theta_0,

\mathbb{E}\!\left[\varphi_0(Z)\,(Y - D^\top \theta_0)\right] = 0,

which, together with a rank condition, identifies \theta_0 when \varphi_0 is known. A crucial convenience from representation-learning theory is that we don’t need \varphi_0 exactly: any bijective transformation of a valid instrument is still a valid instrument, and any rank-preserving affine transformation of an identifying instrument still identifies \theta_0. This is exactly what representation learning can deliver, so the loose guarantees of disentanglement are tight enough for valid causal inference.

title: Addressing Instrument–Outcome Confounding in Mendelian Randomization through Representation Learning
text:
Identifying the invariant component
The recovery is driven by distributional invariance. We train an autoencoder (m_{\text{en}}, m_{\text{de}}) that reconstructs Z, and require the first \hat{p} encoder coordinates to have a distribution that is stable across environments:

\forall\, k, k' \in [K], \quad
m_{\text{en}}(Z^{(k)})^{:\hat{p}} \stackrel{d}{=} m_{\text{en}}(Z^{(k')})^{:\hat{p}}.

Reconstruction forces the representation to preserve the information in Z, and invariance forces the first block to track the environment-stable signal. Under injective polynomial mixing1 and a modular, sufficiently-variable shift in the distribution of V, we have:
1 We foreground the polynomial case here because it yields the strongest, cleanest guarantee — exact affine recovery of W. The paper treats identifiability more generally: see the margin note on general C^1-diffeomorphic mixing, alongside the linear and misspecified-dimension analyses.
If \hat{p} \ge p, the encoder’s first \hat{p} coordinates perfectly identify W, recovering it up to an affine transformation m_{\text{en}}(Z^{(k)})^{:\hat{p}} = A\,W^{(k)} + a. If \hat{p} < p, W is partially identified (recovered up to a linear projection).

Compared to prior multi-environment causal representation learning (Ahuja et al. 2024), our approach does not require an additive-noise SCM over the latents or that interventions act only on exogenous noise, and we explicitly work out what happens when the latent dimension is misspecified. It also connects to the invariance-principle view of representation learning (Yao et al. 2025) and to the broader identifiability literature (Khemakhem et al. 2020; Locatello et al. 2019), while contrasting with earlier learned-representation IV methods that lacked recovery guarantees (Cheng et al. 2024a, 2024b).

Ahuja, Kartik, Amin Mansouri, and Yixin Wang. 2024. “Multi-Domain Causal Representation Learning via Weak Distributional Invariances.” International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), 865–73.

Yao, Dingling, Dario Rancati, Riccardo Cadei, Marco Fumero, and Francesco Locatello. 2025. “Unifying Causal Representation Learning with the Invariance Principle.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Khemakhem, Ilyes, Diederik P. Kingma, Ricardo Pio Monti, and Aapo Hyvärinen. 2020. “Variational Autoencoders and Nonlinear ICA: A Unifying Framework.” International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), 2207–17.

Locatello, Francesco, Stefan Bauer, Mario Lucic, et al. 2019. “Challenging Common Assumptions in the Unsupervised Learning of Disentangled Representations.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 4114–24.

Cheng, Debo, Ziqi Xu, Jiuyong Li, Lin Liu, Jixue Liu, and Thuc Duy Le. 2024a. “Conditional Instrumental Variable Regression with Representation Learning for Causal Inference.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Cheng, Debo, Ziqi Xu, Jiuyong Li, Lin Liu, Jixue Liu, and Thuc Duy Le. 2024b. “Disentangled Representation Learning for Causal Inference with Instruments.” IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems 35 (8): 1–14.
The invalid block V is not identifiable in general, even when W is perfectly recovered. Under polynomial mixing, adding an independence constraint between the two encoder blocks recovers both W and V up to affine transformations.
In practice the autoencoder minimizes a weighted sum of a reconstruction loss, an invariance loss, and an independence loss. We use Maximum Mean Discrepancy (Gretton et al. 2012) for invariance and the Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion (Gretton et al. 2005) for independence, with a term that discourages representation collapse.

Gretton, Arthur, Karsten M. Borgwardt, Malte J. Rasch, Bernhard Schölkopf, and Alexander J. Smola. 2012. “A Kernel Two-Sample Test.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 13 (25): 723–73.

Gretton, Arthur, Olivier Bousquet, Alex Smola, and Bernhard Schölkopf. 2005. “Measuring Statistical Dependence with Hilbert–Schmidt Norms.” Algorithmic Learning Theory (ALT), 63–78.

title: Addressing Instrument–Outcome Confounding in Mendelian Randomization through Representation Learning
section: Good and bad uses of the learned representation
text:
Good and bad uses of the learned representation
Once W is the instrument, what about V? Because V is correlated with Y (through H) but independent of W, in the ideal case where the true latents are observed it is a valid adjustment covariate: partialling it out reduces the asymptotic variance of the IV estimator. But with learned proxies \widehat{W}, \widehat{V} two risks appear:

Efficiency loss via information leakage — if disentanglement is imperfect, \widehat{V} may absorb part of W, weakening the first stage and inflating variance.
Bias via a collider — if the independence constraint fails, \widehat{V} can become a function of both W and H; conditioning on it opens a backdoor path and biases the estimator.

This is why the independence constraint is not optional for the variance-reduction trick: recovering W for plain IV needs invariance, but safely using V needs independence too.

title: Addressing Instrument–Outcome Confounding in Mendelian Randomization through Representation Learning
text:
Experiments
Semi-synthetic, from All of Us. We extract 652 genetic variants in the GLP1R region from individuals of East Asian and African predicted ancestry (8000 individuals per population), apply ICA to reduce to 10 latent components, pick the component with the strongest cross-population shift as the confounder V, and resample the rest as the invariant W — then map back to SNP space so the genotypes keep realistic LD but carry controlled stratification. A two-dimensional exposure D and scalar outcome Y follow a linear SCM with an unobserved confounder H copied from V; we repeat over 20 seeds.
Training the autoencoder with \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = 10, we build two estimators on the learned representation: \text{2SLS}(\widehat{W}) and the partialling-out variant \text{PO}(\widehat{V})\text{-2SLS}(\widehat{W}). They are compared against naive \text{2SLS}(Z), MR-Egger (Bowden et al. 2015), and their population-label-adjusted counterparts \text{PO}(K)\text{-2SLS}(Z) and \text{PO}(K)\text{-Egger}(Z).

Bowden, Jack, George Davey Smith, and Stephen Burgess. 2015. “Mendelian Randomization with Invalid Instruments: Effect Estimation and Bias Detection Through Egger Regression.” International Journal of Epidemiology 44 (2): 512–25.
The reported qualitative findings are collected in Table 1 (the paper presents them as box-plots of bias over the 20 seeds).

Two messages stand out. First, partialling out the discrete population label (\text{PO}(K)) helps but does not remove the bias, showing the confounding is more than a mean shift between populations. Second, the partialling-out estimator that adjusts for the learned \widehat{V} has visibly tighter variance than plain \text{2SLS}(\widehat{W}) — the predicted efficiency gain.
Fully-synthetic ablations. With p = q = 2 and noise drawn from correlated Gaussians, we vary the mixing function across polynomials of degree 1–3 (giving d_Z \in \{5, 15, 35\}) and an invertible MLP (d_Z = 4):

Mixing mechanism. Both proposed estimators stay at low or near-zero bias across all four mixing functions, while every baseline shows large bias — standard IV and population-adjusted variants fail once the mixing is non-linear or the invalidity is latent rather than a discrete label.
Misspecified dimension. With the true p = 2 and degree-3 polynomial mixing, we sweep \hat{p} \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}. Under-specifying (\hat{p}=1, where a linear projection of W still suffices for valid IV), correctly specifying, and even moderately over-specifying (\hat{p}=3) all keep bias small; only strong over-specification (\hat{p}=4) raises both bias and variance as the model leaks information from V — so a conservative dimension is preferable when the instrument is still strong.
Independence loss. With the independence loss, both estimators are unbiased. Without it (\lambda_2 = 0), \text{2SLS}(\widehat{W}) stays largely unbiased but \text{PO}(\widehat{V})\text{-2SLS}(\widehat{W}) picks up significant bias, worst under the complex Poly-3 and MLP mixings — confirming that the adjustment trick requires disentanglement.

title: Addressing Instrument–Outcome Confounding in Mendelian Randomization through Representation Learning
text:
Why it matters
This paper reframes a long-standing epidemiological headache — invalid instruments from population structure — as a causal representation learning problem, and shows that cross-environment invariance is enough to recover the exogenous part of a confounded instrument up to a transformation that downstream IV estimation can absorb. The honest accounting of when the learned invalid component helps (variance reduction) versus hurts (leakage, collider bias) is the practical payoff. Limitations we flag: the guarantees rest on a sufficient-variability assumption whose finite-sample testing is open, and high-dimensional genetic settings would benefit from sparsity in the encoder. We also note the framework extends from multi-environment to multi-view data, where a contrastive objective such as InfoNCE (Oord et al. 2018) could replace the MMD invariance loss.



Oord, Aaron van den, Yazhe Li, and Oriol Vinyals. 2018. “Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1807.03748.

title: About
text:
Modern machine learning is still limited to a superficial description of reality that only holds when the experimental conditions are fixed. It largely ignores interventions in the world, domain shifts, and temporal structure. Our group focuses on learning causal representations and causal models from data to address these issues. Through rigorous theory and scalable algorithms, we enable AI agents to understand cause-and-effect relationships, the effect of interventions, and distribution changes underlying the data they encounter.
Advances in causal learning have promising applications in machine learning and artificial intelligence, including robustness, explainability, and fairness in recognition, reasoning, and planning tasks. Most importantly, their impact extends to discovering new scientific knowledge from massive amounts of data and serving as the interface between people and complex systems for decision-making.
Causal learning emerges by discovering structural knowledge about the data-generating process and meaningful abstractions that allow for well-defined causal relations. Research questions span theoretical identifiability and methodological innovations in causal learning, discovering objects and abstract entities, their factors of variations, and their causal relations. We apply these methods to solve open problems in machine learning and enable new applications in the sciences.

title: Controlling Transient Amplification Improves Long-horizon Rollouts
section: The gap between one step and many
text:
The gap between one step and many
Neural networks are increasingly used to simulate physical systems — the weather, ocean currents, turbulent fluids, molecules. The common recipe is to train a network to take one small step forward in time: given the state of the system now, predict what it looks like a moment later. To forecast far into the future, you simply run the network in a loop, feeding each prediction back in as the next input. Trained this way, these models have become remarkably accurate and often run orders of magnitude faster than the classical solvers they imitate (Pathak et al. 2022; Lam et al. 2023; Kochkov et al. 2024; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al. 2020).

Lam, Remi, Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez, Matthew Willson, et al. 2023. “Learning Skillful Medium-Range Global Weather Forecasting.” Science 382 (6677). https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adi2336.

Kochkov, Dmitrii, Janni Yuval, Ian Langmore, et al. 2024. “Neural General Circulation Models for Weather and Climate.” Nature 632: 1060–66.

Sanchez-Gonzalez, Alvaro, Jonathan Godwin, Tobias Pfaff, Rex Ying, Jure Leskovec, and Peter W. Battaglia. 2020. “Learning to Simulate Complex Physics with Graph Networks.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML).
The trouble is the loop itself. Each prediction carries a small error, and as the model consumes its own output step after step, accuracy degrades far faster than the single-step error would suggest: a model that nearly matches the ground truth after one step can drift or blow up within tens of steps (Lippe et al. 2023). Closing this gap between one step and many is the central open problem for neural simulators of dynamics.
The usual explanation is distributional shift — the model trains on clean data but rolls out on its own imperfect outputs, which slowly wander off the training distribution. Methods that expose the model to its own errors during training (Lippe et al. 2023) or correct predictions at inference (Kohl et al. 2026) help, but they treat drift as a data or inference problem. They do not explain the structural mechanism that makes a small error grow in the first place. This work is complementary to those methods, not a replacement: it targets the structural component of error growth, and the two should combine.

Lippe, Phillip, Bastiaan S. Veeling, Paris Perdikaris, Richard E. Turner, and Johannes Brandstetter. 2023. “PDE-Refiner: Achieving Accurate Long Rollouts with Neural PDE Solvers.” Thirty-Seventh Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS). https://openreview.net/forum?id=Qv6468llWS.

Kohl, Georg, Li-Wei Chen, and Nils Thuerey. 2026. “Benchmarking Autoregressive Conditional Diffusion Models for Turbulent Flow Simulation.” Neural Networks 199: 108641. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2026.108641.

title: Controlling Transient Amplification Improves Long-horizon Rollouts
text:
Transient amplification
The mechanism we point to is a classical phenomenon from dynamical systems called transient amplification. The idea is best seen on a simple stable system perturbed away from equilibrium. Asymptotic stability only guarantees that the perturbation eventually dies out — it says nothing about what happens on the way there.









Figure 1: Stable. Orthogonal directions of decay (a normal system). The perturbation shrinks monotonically.













Figure 2: Unstable. One direction genuinely grows. The perturbation diverges without bound.













Figure 3: Transient. The same stable eigenvalues as the first case, but nearly parallel directions (a non-normal system). The norm first grows to a peak well above its starting value before decaying.






All three systems above are built from the same kind of linear update; what differs is the geometry of their directions and whether they grow or shrink. The first two cases are the familiar ones. When the directions are orthogonal and contracting (a stable, normal system), a perturbation simply decays. When one direction genuinely grows (an unstable system), the perturbation diverges without bound — the obvious failure mode, and the one stability analysis is built to rule out.
The third case is the subtle one, and the point of this work. It has the same stable eigenvalues as the first, so it is still asymptotically stable — it always returns to equilibrium. But its directions are nearly parallel (a non-normal system), and on the way back, the nearly-cancelling projections briefly reinforce one another and the perturbation is amplified, sometimes by a large factor, before it decays (Trefethen and Embree 2005). A system can be perfectly stable and still blow a small error up by a large factor first. This is exactly the regime that matters in practice, because rollouts are judged at tens to hundreds of steps — the medium horizon where transients dominate. Enforcing stability alone does not protect against it.

Trefethen, Lloyd N., and Mark Embree. 2005. Spectra and Pseudospectra: The Behavior of Nonnormal Matrices and Operators. Princeton University Press.

title: Controlling Transient Amplification Improves Long-horizon Rollouts
section: From dynamical systems to neural networks
text:
From dynamical systems to neural networks
The same picture transfers to a neural simulator through linearization. Following its prediction error from one step to the next, the error is advanced by the model’s local Jacobian — the linear map describing how the network responds to a small change in its input. Over a rollout the error is therefore passed through a product of these Jacobians, one per step, and it is the behavior of this product that decides whether errors stay small or amplify.
Two properties of those Jacobians keep transients in check. First, each Jacobian should be close to normal, so that no single step amplifies errors (the within-step story above). Second, the Jacobians at successive steps should commute, so their directions of stretching stay aligned over time; otherwise a direction that one step contracts can be re-expanded by the next. Standard training rewards neither property, and unregularized networks trained on non-normal dynamics tend to learn Jacobians that are both non-normal and non-commuting.
Commutativity regularization adds two penalties during training to encourage exactly these properties: a normality penalty on each latent Jacobian and a commutator penalty on consecutive Jacobians. The two are complementary — controlling one without the other leaves either within-step or cross-step amplification uncontrolled. Both are estimated cheaply with Jacobian-vector products, never forming any matrix explicitly, and the rollout at inference is unchanged, so there is no inference-time cost. A propagator bound in the paper makes this precise: as the penalties shrink, long-horizon error decays at the rate set by the Jacobians’ spectral radius rather than their (generally larger) spectral norm. We refer the reader to the paper for the full method and theory.







Figure 4: Commutativity regularization acts on the latent advance map \mathbf{z}_t \mapsto \mathbf{z}_{t+1} (the U-Net bottleneck, or the middle FNO layers), leaving the inference path untouched.

title: Controlling Transient Amplification Improves Long-horizon Rollouts
text:
Long-horizon rollouts in practice
We evaluate the regularizer across settings spanning 1D and 2D, integrable and chaotic, synthetic and real. In each case an otherwise-identical baseline is compared against a model with the two penalties added, and rollouts are run far beyond the training window. The recurring trade: a small amount of one-step accuracy is exchanged for a bounded, far more accurate long-horizon rollout.
KdV (1D). Trained on a short window of single-soliton dynamics and rolled out to many times that horizon, the regularized U-Net stays accurate where the baseline drifts. The effect is sharpest out-of-distribution: on initial conditions with several interacting solitons — never seen in training — the baseline degrades badly while the regularized model is largely unaffected.





In-distribution — initial condition (single soliton)







In-distribution — U-Net (baseline)






In-distribution — U-Net + Comm. Reg. (ours)








Out-of-distribution — initial condition (multiple solitons)







Out-of-distribution — U-Net (baseline)






Out-of-distribution — U-Net + Comm. Reg. (ours)








Barotropic vorticity (2D, chaotic). On this dissipative, chaotic fluid the unregularized U-Net destabilizes inside the training horizon, saturating into a field decorrelated from the truth. The same regularizer that controls slow drift on KdV here converts an instability into a bounded, on-attractor rollout.





Barotropic vorticity rollout: ground truth, baseline, and regularized U-Net.



FourCastNet on ERA5 (real, large-scale). Starting from the pretrained FourCastNet weather model (Pathak et al. 2022), we fine-tune on a few in-distribution years of its own training data. Plain fine-tuning worsens the long-horizon near-surface temperature forecast; the same data with commutativity regularization turns that regression into a substantial improvement over the frozen model — no new data, no inference-time cost.

Pathak, Jaideep, Shashank Subramanian, Peter Harrington, et al. 2022. “FourCastNet: A Global Data-Driven High-Resolution Weather Model Using Adaptive Fourier Neural Operators.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2202.11214. https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.11214.





Near-surface temperature (t_\mathrm{2m}) rollout error on held-out ERA5: frozen vs. plain fine-tune vs. regularized fine-tune.

title: Controlling Transient Amplification Improves Long-horizon Rollouts
text:
Takeaways
Long-horizon rollout error is not only a data problem. A stable neural simulator can still amplify its own errors transiently, and non-normal, non-commuting latent Jacobians are a structural driver of that amplification — one that enforcing stability alone does not address. Commutativity regularization controls the mechanism directly with two Jacobian-vector-product penalties at zero inference cost, and it is complementary to refinement and diffusion methods that target distributional shift. For the propagator bound, the full method, and the complete experiments, we invite you to read the paper.

Controlling Transient Amplification Improves Long-horizon Rollouts



AI for Science

Dynamical Systems

Theory



Autoregressive neural simulators match classical solvers on short-horizon prediction but degrade rapidly over long rollouts. This work identifies transient amplification of perturbations along rollout trajectories as a structural driver of that error: when the Jacobians along an autoregressive trajectory are non-normal and non-commuting, errors are amplified transiently even when the system is asymptotically stable. The authors propose commutativity regularization — a commutator penalty and a normality penalty, both estimated with Jacobian-vector products and carrying no inference-time cost — and prove a propagator bound that replaces the per-step spectral-norm decay rate with the shared spectral radius under approximate commutativity and normality. On UNet and FNO variants across the 1D KdV equation, the 2D barotropic vorticity equation, sea-surface temperature, and fine-tuning of FourCastNet on ERA5, the method sustains long-horizon rollouts over thousands of steps, with the largest gains out-of-distribution.

Addressing Instrument–Outcome Confounding in Mendelian Randomization through Representation Learning



Causal Inference

Representation Learning

AI for Science



Mendelian Randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instruments to estimate causal effects from observational data, but its core assumptions — especially the independence between instruments and unobserved confounders — are routinely broken by population stratification and assortative mating. Leveraging the growing availability of multi-environment biobank data, this work proposes a representation-learning framework that exploits cross-environment invariance to recover the latent exogenous component of a confounded genetic instrument. It provides identifiability guarantees for recovering these latent instruments under several mixing mechanisms, and demonstrates effective bias correction in simulations and in semi-synthetic experiments built from the All of Us Research Hub.
